**Estimating project effort and scope**
**Analyzing product validation and search engine capabilities**

I’m sorting through validation goals like query accuracy and product labeling, while examining Meili and alternatives for search API and pricing filter support. I’m cautious about license uncertainties, deployment constraints, and dependency claims, aiming to back everything with solid URLs and avoid assumptions about existing databases or forbidden technologies.

{
  "answer_markdown": "**Evaluate Meilisearch (ID `130688011`) first for your product-search prototype.** Its documented application search, typo tolerance and facets directly address shoppers mistyping product names and narrowing results by brand. The supplied host read dated **2026-10-11** supports this preference, while explicitly leaving indexing, synchronization and relevance validation to your team. Better product discovery is an expected benefit to test, not a measured result. [Meilisearch repository](https://github.com/meilisearch/meilisearch)

This is a **conditional recommendation for validation**, rather than approval for complete adoption. The supplied evidence does not establish numeric price-range filtering, suitability for your catalog size and languages, hosting compatibility, or the license terms of the exact version you would deploy. In particular, facets alone do not prove that the required price-filter behavior works. Typesense remains excluded.

**Proposed architecture and technical work**

Retain whichever system currently owns your product records and the existing application. Add Meilisearch as a derived search index, with a small JavaScript integration layer:

`Product source → initial export + update/delete synchronization → Meilisearch index`

`Shopper UI → application search endpoint → Meilisearch → product results + filter information`

The application endpoint is a proposed boundary for validating queries and enforcing any visibility rules. Keep indexing/admin credentials on the server. Index only fields shoppers may see; use the authoritative product source to confirm current price and availability when purchasing. This avoids treating a potentially stale search result as transaction authority.

Meilisearch would cover the search-engine role. Your developer would still own the product-document mapping, brand normalization, numeric price representation, synchronization, search UI, relevance tuning and operational checks. The supplied host observation explicitly identifies indexing, synchronization and relevance validation as remaining project work. [Meilisearch repository](https://github.com/meilisearch/meilisearch)

For shoppers, the proposed outcome is a search box that can recover from common spelling mistakes and allow useful narrowing of results. Whether that actually helps depends on your product names, brands and real query patterns. Semantic search is not established as a requirement, so it should stay outside the first slice.

**Comparison with the other transmitted options and the current solution**

| Option | Assessment for this project | Condition that could change the choice |
|---|---|---|
| **Meilisearch** | Best-supported first validation candidate: the dated host evidence confirms typo tolerance and facets. | Required price filtering, relevance, license or deployment checks fail. |
| **OpenSearch / Elasticsearch** | The frozen cards identify distributed search engines. A broader engine may be appropriate, but these materials do not establish a better fit for this prototype. Mapping, query design and operations would need investigation. | You already operate one, or demonstrate requirements the simpler candidate cannot meet. |
| **Vespa** | The frozen card identifies an AI search platform; the supplied evidence does not resolve the specific typo-tolerance and brand/price workflow. There is no demonstrated reason to introduce that platform scope yet. | A concrete advanced ranking or serving requirement justifies it, and product-search fit is verified. |
| **Crawlee** | Its documented role is crawling and browser automation. Your requirement is search over your own catalog, so it does not supply the required search-engine role. | A separate ingestion need emerges; that would still require a search component. |
| **SereneDB** | The frozen card describes a search analytics database, but the required shopper-search behavior remains unverified. Catalog acceptance does not establish application fit. | A pilot proves the required matching and filters and identifies a relevant architectural advantage. |

These comparisons use the supplied frozen cards, not fresh checks of those alternatives. Sources: [OpenSearch](https://github.com/opensearch-project/OpenSearch), [Elasticsearch](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch), [Vespa](https://github.com/vespa-engine/vespa), [Crawlee](https://github.com/apify/crawlee), [SereneDB](https://github.com/serenedb/serenedb). They are alternatives or out-of-scope references, not a set to install together.

Keeping your current/native search could be preferable if it already provides acceptable typo recovery and filters. That would avoid another service and synchronization path. Its capabilities are unknown here, so the first validation should compare against it if available. Reuse introduces dependency upgrades, hosting, index recovery and freshness monitoring; custom development introduces ownership of matching, ranking and filter correctness. Reuse does not automatically win.

**Conditional effort estimate**

For planning only, assume one JavaScript developer familiar with the application and HTTP integrations, an accessible product export and update mechanism, at most roughly 10,000 products, one language/currency, public product visibility, and an available deployment environment. Scope is one search UI with typo handling, brand/price filters, synchronization and basic operational recovery. It excludes high availability, personalized pricing, semantic search and a platform migration. Confidence is low to moderate until validation.

| Phase | Meilisearch integration | Equivalent-scope custom search |
|---|---:|---:|
| First validation / baseline and design | 6–10 engineer-hours | 6–10 engineer-hours |
| Matching, ranking and filter implementation | 4–8 | 24–48 |
| Product mapping and update/delete synchronization | 8–16 | 8–16 |
| Application endpoint and search UI | 10–18 | 10–18 |
| Regression checks, recovery and rollout/rollback preparation | 8–14 | 12–24 |
| **Total, including first validation once** | **36–66 engineer-hours** | **60–116 engineer-hours** |

At **8 engineer-hours per engineer-day**, with that developer allocated full time and phases performed sequentially, these scenarios imply **4.5–8.25 working days** for integration and **7.5–14.5 working days** for custom development. The custom estimate means application-specific search over this bounded catalog, not building a general search platform. Neither range is a commitment or measured saving. Hosting procurement, license decisions and owner feedback add unknown waiting time; part-time allocation extends elapsed time. Ongoing maintenance and provider costs are not quantified.

The main complexity drivers are catalog cleanliness, update frequency, multilingual matching, product variants, customer-specific visibility/prices and deployment ownership. If those assumptions do not hold, the complete-adoption total is unknown until scoped. The most useful scope clarification is: **approximately how many products must be searched, and how are product changes available to the application?**

**Concrete first validation**

Use the 6–10-hour slice to index **500–1,000 representative products**, including similar names, inconsistent brand spellings and price-boundary cases. Create **30–50 owner-labeled queries** covering exact names, common typos, ambiguous terms and combined brand/price filters. Compare against current search if available.

Check that intended products appear in the agreed result positions, filters never return out-of-range or wrong-brand items, and a product update and deletion reach the index within an owner-agreed freshness target. Also check the exact deployment version's license, required runtime/client compatibility and credential boundaries. Agree relevance and latency acceptance targets before judging the results; none have been measured here.

Proceed only if that slice demonstrates the required numeric price filtering, useful relevance and an acceptable synchronization/deployment path. Otherwise retain the current component while investigating the failed requirement. The frozen catalog remains unchanged; the supplied 2026-10-11 host observations are transient answer evidence, and no implementation or validation has been executed.",
